Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

questions.q: Sound of wavelength λ travelling at v m/s enters another medium where its speed is 2v m/s. The new wavelength is —
questions.work:
The frequency does not change, so λ ∝ v.
Speed doubles ⇒ λ' = 2λ.

questions.q: Through wave motion —
options: both energy and particles are transmitted

questions.q: A wave y = A sin(kx − ωt) travels on a string. The maximum particle velocity is —
questions.work: Particle velocity = ∂y/∂t = −Aω cos(kx − ωt); its maximum value is Aω.

questions.q: A boat is rocked by waves whose crests are 100 m apart, moving at 25 m/s. The boat bounces up every —
The ratio of fundamental frequencies of an open pipe and a closed pipe of the same length is —
questions.work: Open: ν = v/2L. Closed: ν = v/4L. Ratio = (v/2L) : (v/4L) = 2 : 1.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: Name the factors on which the speed of a wave on a stretched string depends.
questions.answer: v = √(T/μ): it depends on the tension T in the string and its mass per unit length μ. More tension gives higher speed; a heavier string gives lower speed.

questions.q: 'All harmonics are overtones but all overtones are not harmonics.' Explain.
questions.answer: Harmonics are integral multiples of the fundamental. Overtones are the frequencies actually produced above the fundamental. In a closed pipe only odd harmonics occur, so the first overtone is the 3rd harmonic and the 2nd harmonic is missing. Every overtone is a harmonic, but not every harmonic appears as an overtone.

questions.q: Distinguish between (i) pitch and frequency and (ii) loudness and intensity.
questions.answer:
(i) Frequency is the number of vibrations per second (a physical quantity); pitch is the sensation of shrillness, which depends on frequency.
(ii) Intensity is the energy flowing per second per unit area (∝ amplitude²); loudness is the ear's sensation of it.

questions.q: Give two differences between stationary and travelling waves.
questions.answer:
(1) A travelling wave transfers energy; a stationary wave does not.
(2) In a travelling wave every particle has the same amplitude; in a stationary wave the amplitude varies from zero at nodes to maximum at antinodes.

questions.q: The speed of sound in air at 0 °C is 332 m/s. Find it at 20 °C.
An open pipe of length l₁ and a closed pipe of length l₂ resonate with the same fork in their fundamental modes. Find l₁/l₂.
questions.answer:
Open: ν = v/2l₁. Closed: ν = v/4l₂.
v/2l₁ = v/4l₂ ⇒ l₁ = 2l₂ ⇒ l₁/l₂ = 2.

questions.q: Give two differences between transverse and longitudinal waves.
questions.answer:
(1) In transverse waves particles vibrate perpendicular to the wave direction; in longitudinal waves, along it.
(2) Transverse waves form crests and troughs; longitudinal waves form compressions and rarefactions. Transverse waves can be polarized; longitudinal waves cannot.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: A source of sound of frequency 1 kHz moves towards a stationary observer at 40 m/s. Find the wavelength received when (i) both are at rest and (ii) the source moves. (v = 340 m/s)
questions.answer:
(i) λ = v/ν = 340/1000 = 0.34 m.
(ii) The waves are crowded together: λ' = (v − vₛ)/ν = (340 − 40)/1000 = 0.30 m.
The apparent frequency is 340/0.30 ≈ 1133 Hz.

questions.q: Write Newton's formula for the speed of sound in air. Why and how did Laplace correct it?
questions.answer:
Newton assumed isothermal changes: v = √(P/ρ) ≈ 280 m/s at NTP, much less than the measured 332 m/s.
Laplace pointed out that compressions and rarefactions are so rapid, and air such a poor conductor, that the process is adiabatic. Then the elasticity is γP, so v = √(γP/ρ) = √(1.4 × 1.013 × 10⁵/1.29) ≈ 332 m/s, agreeing with experiment.

questions.q: How is the speed of sound in air affected by temperature, pressure, density and humidity? At what temperature does it become twice its value at 27 °C?
questions.answer:
Temperature: v ∝ √T, so it rises with temperature. Pressure: no effect at constant temperature (P/ρ stays constant). Density: v ∝ 1/√ρ. Humidity: moist air is less dense, so v increases.
For v to double, T must be 4 times: 4 × 300 = 1200 K = 927 °C.

questions.q: What are beats? How are they used to find the unknown frequency of a tuning fork?
questions.answer:
Beats are the periodic rise and fall of loudness when two sounds of slightly different frequencies are heard together. The number of beats per second = ν₁ − ν₂.
Sound the unknown fork with a known fork (ν) and count the beats b: the unknown is ν ± b. Load the unknown fork with wax (lowering its frequency): if the beats increase, it was ν − b; if they decrease, it was ν + b.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: State the Doppler effect. A source emits 5 kHz. Find the frequency received when (i) source and observer are at rest, (ii) the source approaches a stationary observer at 30 m/s, (iii) it recedes at 30 m/s. (v = 330 m/s) Give two applications.
questions.answer:
Doppler effect: the apparent change in frequency of a wave due to relative motion of the source and the observer.
(i) ν = 5000 Hz.
(ii) ν' = νv/(v − vₛ) = 5000 × 330/300 = 5500 Hz.
(iii) ν' = νv/(v + vₛ) = 5000 × 330/360 ≈ 4583 Hz.
Applications: radar and police speed guns; finding the speed of stars from red shift; SONAR; medical ultrasound (blood-flow measurement).

questions.q: Derive the equation of a plane progressive harmonic wave. Show that the particle velocity leads the displacement by π/2.
questions.answer:
The source vibrates as y = A sin ωt. A particle at distance x starts x/v later, so y = A sin ω(t − x/v) = A sin(ωt − kx), with k = ω/v = 2π/λ.
Particle velocity u = ∂y/∂t = Aω cos(ωt − kx) = Aω sin(ωt − kx + π/2).
So the velocity leads the displacement by π/2, and its maximum value is Aω.

questions.q: Explain the formation of stationary waves in an air column. Show that an open pipe gives all harmonics but a closed pipe gives only odd harmonics.
questions.answer:
When a wave is reflected back on itself, the incident and reflected waves superpose to form a stationary wave, y = 2A sin kx cos ωt, with fixed nodes and antinodes λ/2 apart.
Closed pipe: a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4 …, giving ν = v/4L, 3v/4L, 5v/4L — only odd harmonics.
Open pipe: antinodes at both ends, so L = λ/2, λ, 3λ/2 …, giving ν = v/2L, 2v/2L, 3v/2L — all harmonics.
So an open pipe's fundamental is twice that of a closed pipe of the same length.
